question: In trade finance, how do over invoicing, under invoicing and short shipping each transfer excess value, and which party to the trade gains in each case?
summary: I could not substantiate the rejected claim. Repeated searches using varied vocabulary ("short shipping", "seller ships fewer goods than invoiced", "over-/under-shipment", "misrepresentation of quantity", "Short Shipping / Over Shipping / Falsely Described Goods") returned no passage that defines "short shipping" or names the party that gains from it, so I am dropping that claim rather than restating it as a negative finding about the corpus (which no single passage can verify). What the corpus does support is set out below: the Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT methods table defines Phantom Shipping and attributes a gaining party for over-invoicing, under-invoicing and multiple invoicing, and FATF/Egmont, the FATF professional money laundering report and the UK NRA describe phantom/ghost shipping and quantity- and quality-based misrepresentation more generally.

verdicts.claim: The Wolfsberg Group, ICC and BAFT Trade Finance Principles define "Phantom Shipping" as a method in which no goods are shipped and all documentation is completely falsified.
verdicts.detail: The passage states "Phantom Shipping No goods are shipped and all documentation is completely falsified," directly matching the claim's definition.

verdicts.claim: In the Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT methods table, Over Invoicing is described as misrepresenting the price of goods above their true value, so that the seller gains excess value as a result of the payment.
verdicts.detail: The passage states "Over Invoicing: By misrepresenting the price of the goods in the invoice and other documentation (stating it at above the true value) the seller gains excess value as a result of the payment," which directly matches the claim.

verdicts.claim: In the same Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT table, Under Invoicing is described as misrepresenting the price of goods below their true value, so that the buyer gains excess value when payment is made.
verdicts.detail: The passage states exactly this: "Under Invoicing By misrepresenting the price of the goods... (stating it as below the true value) the buyer gains excess value when the payment is made."

verdicts.claim: The Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT table describes Multiple Invoicing as issuing more than one invoice for the same goods so a seller can justify the receipt of multiple payments, which is harder to detect if the colluding parties use more than one financial institution.
verdicts.detail: The passage states verbatim: 'By issuing more than one invoice for the same goods a seller can justify the receipt of multiple payments. This will be harder to detect if the colluding parties use more than one FI to facilitate the payments and or transactions.'

verdicts.claim: The Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT Principles state that trade finance methods used to obscure the illegal movement of funds include misrepresenting the price, quality or quantity of goods, and generally rely on collusion between seller and buyer, sometimes because both parties are controlled by the same persons.
verdicts.detail: The passage states verbatim: "The use of Trade Finance to obscure the illegal movement of funds includes methods to misrepresent the price, quality or quantity of goods. Generally, these techniques rely upon collusion between the seller and buyer... The collusion may arise because both parties are controlled by the same persons."

verdicts.claim: FATF/Egmont report that more sophisticated money laundering networks may use phantom shipping in conjunction with multiple invoices, with one shipment of actual goods creating a veneer of legitimacy while subsequent trading uses multiple invoices for phantom shipments.
verdicts.detail: The passage states "more sophisticated ML networks may use phantom shipping in conjunction with multiple invoices. One shipment may involve the movement of actual goods to create a veneer of legitimacy... with subsequent trading may uses multiple invoices for phantom shipments," matching the claim's specifics.

verdicts.claim: The FATF Professional Money Laundering report describes "phantom shipments" as transfers of funds that purport to relate to trade or to the purchase of goods that are ultimately never shipped or received.
verdicts.detail: The passage states "The transfer of funds which purport to be related to trade, or to the purchase of goods that are ultimately never shipped or received (also known as 'phantom shipments')", matching the claim exactly.

verdicts.claim: The FATF Professional Money Laundering report describes falsifying the number and/or value of goods being shipped to be higher or lower than the corresponding payment as a TBML variation, referring to it as over- or under-invoicing.
verdicts.detail: The passage lists "Falsifying the number and/or value of goods being shipped to be higher or lower than the corresponding payment... (also known as over or under-invoicing)" as one of the TBML variations.

verdicts.claim: The UK National Risk Assessment 2025 lists "fictitious trading (also known as ghost or phantom shipping)" among the processes criminals use to integrate criminal funds into trade, alongside mis-declaration of goods, over- and under-invoicing, mis-stating the quality or type of good, and issuing multiple invoices for the same transaction.
verdicts.detail: The passage lists exactly these items under "processes currently employed by criminals to integrate criminal funds into trade": mis-declaration/over-under-invoicing, mis-stating quality or type of good, issuing multiple invoices for the same transaction, and "Fictious trading (also known as ghost or phantom shipping)".

drafts.question: In trade finance, how do over invoicing, under invoicing and short shipping each transfer excess value, and which party to the trade gains in each case?
drafts.summary: The corpus (principally the Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT Trade Finance Principles and the FATF/Egmont TBML reports) clearly explains over-invoicing and under-invoicing as price-misrepresentation techniques, and identifies which party gains in each: the seller in over-invoicing, the buyer in under-invoicing. Both rely on collusion between buyer and seller, since the object is to obtain a benefit beyond what an arm's-length transaction would yield. "Short shipping" as a named technique is NOT defined in the retrieved corpus. The nearest documented shipment-side technique is "phantom shipping", where no goods are shipped at all and the documentation is wholly falsified; the guidance also notes that misrepresentation of the quantity (as well as price and quality) of goods is a route by which value is transferred, but it does not spell out which party gains from short shipping.

claims.text: Over-invoicing works by misrepresenting the price of the goods in the invoice and other documentation, stating it above the true value; the seller gains the excess value as a result of the payment.
Under-invoicing works by misrepresenting the price of the goods in the invoice and other documentation, stating it below the true value; the buyer gains the excess value when payment is made.

The key element of over- and under-invoicing is misrepresentation of the price of the good or service in order to transfer value, and the critical enabling aspect is that the importer and exporter are complicit in the misrepresentation.

These trade finance techniques generally rely on collusion between seller and buyer, because the intended outcome is a benefit in excess of what would be expected from an arm's-length transaction; the collusion may arise because both parties are controlled by the same persons.
Value can be transferred by misrepresenting the price, quality or quantity of goods, not only the price.

The corpus does not define 'short shipping' or attribute a gaining party to it; the shipment-side technique it does define is phantom shipping, in which no goods are shipped and all documentation is completely falsified.

A related technique documented in the corpus is multiple invoicing, where a seller issues more than one invoice for the same goods to justify receipt of multiple payments, which is harder to detect if the colluding parties use more than one financial institution.

Whether over-invoicing or under-invoicing (or other misrepresentation of value) exists cannot easily be identified from the trade documents alone, and financial institutions are generally not positioned to judge the legitimacy of unit pricing because most products are not traded on public markets and relevant business information (terms of the relationship, volume discounting, quality of goods) is lacking.

UK national risk assessment guidance similarly lists over- and under-invoicing as misrepresentation of the price of goods or services to transfer value, alongside mis-stating the quality or type of good to justify value differences and fictitious (ghost or phantom) trading.
